_about: Concept ladder for the Learn stage. One concept per rung. Rung ids are progress keys: never rename. skills are glossary.json ids that move to Practiced when the check is passed. goals maps checkpoint data-ids to the rungs (1-based) that teach them. lang: c programs are compiled and run to verify each check.

rungs.title: Functions: parameters and return values
rungs.builds: Phase 2 and 2.5: variables, if and loops. Everything so far has lived inside main.
rungs.why: Your guessing game is one long main. As programs grow that becomes impossible to read. A function packs one job into a named block you can call whenever you need it: inputs go in, one result comes out.

parts: One job, one name

A function is a block of code with a name. You write it once, then call it by name whenever you need that job done. Two words get mixed up all the time. A parameter is the variable in the function's first line: points in int add_score(int score, int points). An argument is the value you hand over when you call it: the 10 in add_score(score, 10). Parameters are the slots, arguments are what goes in them.
What one call does

Every call, however big, runs the same four steps:

  1. C works out each argument, so add_score(score, 5 * 2) becomes 0 and 10.
  2. Each value is copied into its parameter, in order.
  3. The body runs until it reaches a return (or the closing brace of a void function).
  4. The call is replaced by the returned value, and the calling line carries on with it.

That's why the program below can call add_score twice and get a different answer each time: each call starts again from step 1 with new values.
Writing the first line

The first line gives the return type, the name, then the parameters in brackets. Each parameter needs its own type: int add(int a, b) doesn't build, int add(int a, int b) does. A function hands back one value, such as an int, a float or a char. It can't hand back a whole array, and you can't write one function inside another: every function sits on its own at the outer level of the file.

return ends the function on the spot, even halfway through a loop. Anything after it in that path never runs. A function can have several returns, one per way out:

int clamp_hp(int hp) {
    if (hp < 0) {
        return 0;
    }
    return hp;
}
Beginner mistakes

Writing print_menu; without brackets doesn't call anything. It names the function and throws the name away. The brackets are what make it a call, even when they're empty: print_menu();.

A non-void function that can reach its closing brace without a return hands back garbage. In clamp_hp above, delete the last return hp; and any hp of 0 or more falls off the end.

And a return value nobody stores is lost. The check below is about exactly that.
Ending the whole program with exit

return leaves the current function. exit, from <stdlib.h>, ends the whole program from anywhere, however deep you are:

if (lives < 0) {
    printf("Bad save file\n");
    exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
}

EXIT_FAILURE is 1 on Windows and EXIT_SUCCESS is 0, the same codes return in main sends. Run the program, then type echo %ERRORLEVEL% in the terminal: it prints 1. build.bat reads the same %ERRORLEVEL% after cl runs, to see whether the build worked.
MSVC notes

The bracket-less print_menu; is C4550 (the expression is a function with its argument list missing). A path with no return is C4715 (not all control paths return a value). Both are warnings, so /WX stops the build, which is what you want: each one is a real bug.

walk: The first line names the function. int at the front is what it hands back. Inside the brackets are its inputs, called parameters, each with a type.
Inside, score and points are ordinary variables holding whatever was passed in.
return hands the result back to whoever called the function, and ends it.
Calling it: add_score(score, 10) runs the function with score = 0 and points = 10. The result, 10, goes back into score.
Called again with the new score: 10 + 5.
Prints 15.
rungs.model: Mental model: a vending machine. You put inputs in the slot, it does its job where you can’t see, and one thing drops out. main doesn’t need to know how, only what to put in and what comes out.

check.q: What would print if line 11 were add_score(score, 5); with no score = in front?
check.hint: The function returns a value. If nobody catches it, where does it go?
check.why: The function still returns 15, but nothing stores it, so score stays 10. A return value you don’t assign is thrown away.

miss.0: The function can’t change score by itself. Only the score = on the left does that.
miss.1: 5 is the points, not the total.

tryit.task: Write a function that returns the bigger of two ints.

qa: Can a function return two things?
Not directly. One value comes back. Phase 3.5 shows how pointers and structs get around that.
Do parameter names have to match the caller’s variables?
No. add_score(lives, 1) works fine. The value is copied into the parameter, whatever it’s called.
How long should a function be?
Short enough to describe in one sentence. If you need “and” to describe it, it’s probably two functions.
Is return 0 in main the same as return in my function?
Separate things. return total; in your function hands a result to the line that called it. return 0; in main tells the operating system the program finished without errors.
Does defining a function run it?
No. Writing a function only describes it. Nothing happens until a line calls it, and the program always starts at main.
rungs.bridge: You can write a function. Next: void and prototypes: functions that return nothing, and telling the compiler a function exists before you use it.

rungs.title: void and function prototypes
rungs.why: Some functions just do a job, like printing a menu, and have nothing to hand back: that’s void. And C reads top to bottom, so if main calls a function written below it, the compiler needs a one-line heads-up first: the prototype.

parts: Declare first, define later

C reads your file from the top down. When main calls a function written further down, the compiler hasn't met it yet. A prototype fixes that: the function's first line with a ; instead of a body. The definition, with the body, can then go anywhere below.
What a prototype buys you

With the prototype in place, the compiler checks every call against it. Too many or too few arguments stops the build. Each argument is converted to the parameter's type, so passing 2.9f to an int parameter chops it to 2, and /W4 warns C4244, the same chop you met in Variables and types. The prototype and the definition must agree on the return type and every parameter type. If they don't, the build fails at the definition.
The usual file order

Most C files follow one layout, top to bottom: #include lines, then #defines, then prototypes, then main, then the other function definitions. Anyone opening the file sees the list of functions before the detail. In Organising Code (Phase 3.75), the prototypes move into a .h file and the layout stays the same.
Keep writing (void)

In C17, which MSVC follows, empty brackets in a prototype mean “arguments not specified”, so void print_menu(); lets print_menu(5) through unchecked. C23 changed () to mean “no arguments”, as in C++, and you'll see it in newer code. Keep writing (void): it means none on every compiler. Calling a function with no prototype above it is C4013.

walk: A prototype: the function’s first line with a ; instead of a body. It tells the compiler “print_menu exists, takes nothing, returns nothing”.
Another prototype. Now main can call square even though its body is further down.
Calling a void function: no value comes back, so there’s nothing to store.
square(4) runs and hands back 16, which printf prints.
The real function, with its body. void at the front: returns nothing. (void) in the brackets: takes nothing.
Matches its prototype exactly: same name, same types.
rungs.model: Mental model: a prototype is a contents-page entry. The compiler reads the contents first, so when main mentions a function on page 3, it already knows that chapter exists.

check.q: You delete line 4 (the square prototype) and run build.bat (/W4 /WX). What happens?
opts: The build fails at line 8: square isn’t known yet
It builds fine and prints 16 as before
The build fails at line 16, where square is defined
It builds, runs, and prints 0 instead of 16
check.hint: When the compiler reaches line 8, has it seen square yet?
check.why: At line 8 the compiler hasn’t met square, so MSVC warns C4013 (“square undefined; assuming extern returning int”). /WX turns that into a failed build. Prototypes at the top prevent it.

miss.1: Without /WX it might build, with warning C4013. With your flags it fails.
miss.2: Line 16 is fine by itself. The problem is using square before the compiler knows about it.
miss.3: With /WX it never gets as far as running.

tryit.task: Add the missing prototype so main can call heal(), which is written below it.

qa: Why not just put every function above main?
You can, and for small files it’s fine. Prototypes matter once functions call each other, and they’re exactly what goes in a .h file in Organising Code (Phase 3.75).
What does (void) in the brackets mean?
“Takes no inputs.” In C17, empty brackets () mean “not specified”, so the compiler checks nothing. (void) is the precise way to say none, on every compiler.
Can a void function use return?
Yes, a bare return; to leave early. It just can’t return a value.
Why does C need prototypes at all?

C was built to compile in one pass, top to bottom, on machines with very little memory, so a call can only be checked against what it has already read. Newer languages read the whole file first, so they don’t need this. GDScript is one.
rungs.bridge: Your functions can live anywhere in the file. Next: scope: which variables a function can see.

rungs.title: Scope: where a variable lives
rungs.builds: Functions: parameters and return values, and void and function prototypes.
rungs.why: A variable made inside a function only exists inside that function, from its line to the closing }. That’s why two functions can each have a variable called total without clashing, and why a function can’t reach into main’s variables.

parts: Where and how long

Every variable has two properties. Its scope is which lines can use its name. Its lifetime is how long the box exists while the program runs. For a variable declared inside a function, the answers match: the name works from its declaration to the closing } of the block, and the box exists only while that block is running. These are called local variables.
Parameters are local copies

A parameter is a local variable too. On each call it's created and filled with a copy of the argument. In the program below, reset has its own score, separate from main's, and changing it changes nothing back in main. The two don't clash because neither sits inside the other: they're in different functions.
Fresh on every call

Locals are made again each time the function runs and thrown away when it returns. They don't remember last time. And a local you don't initialise holds garbage, whatever bytes were left in that memory:

void take_hit(int damage) {
    int hp;
    hp -= damage;   /* hp was never set: C4700 */
}

Give every local a value on the line that declares it. If you need a value that survives between calls, that's the next concept, Static locals and globals.
Scope starts at the declaration

A name exists from its declaration downwards, not from the top of the block. Use it on an earlier line and you get C2065 (undeclared identifier), even if it's declared two lines later. Blocks inside a function make smaller scopes: a variable declared in the braces of an if or a loop is gone after its }, and the i in for (int i = 0; ...) exists only inside that loop.
Reusing a name breaks the build

C itself allows an inner block to declare a name that's already in use outside it. The inner one hides the outer one until its }:

int lives = 3;
if (hit) {
    int lives = 2;   /* a second lives: C4456 */
    lives--;
}

That compiles in plain C, and the outer lives never changes, which is almost never what you meant. Books (King included) show this as legal. Under your build it isn't.

With /W4 /WX, hiding a name stops the build. C4456: a local hides an earlier local. C4457: a local hides a function parameter. C4459: a local or parameter hides a global. The fix is always a new name.

walk: reset gets its own variable called score: a copy of whatever main passes in.
This changes reset’s copy only.
main’s score. A different variable that happens to share the name.
Passes the value 99 in. reset receives a copy.
main’s score was never touched.
rungs.model: Mental model: each function is its own room. Passing a value in hands over a photocopy. Whatever the function scribbles on its copy, the original in main stays the same.

check.q: What is the second line of output?
opts: A compile error: score is defined twice
Back in main: a garbage number
check.hint: Did reset get main’s variable, or a copy of its value?
check.why: reset changed its own copy to 0. main’s score is a separate variable and stays 99. To change a caller’s variable you need a return value or, in Phase 3.5, a pointer.

miss.0: reset only had a copy. main’s score never changed.
miss.1: Each function has its own score. Same name, different rooms, no clash.
miss.2: main’s score was set to 99 and nothing touched it.

tryit.task: Make reset actually work by returning the new value.

qa: What about variables inside an if or a loop?
Same rule, smaller room. A variable made inside the { } of an if or for disappears at its }. In for (int i = 0; …), i only exists inside that loop.
What are global variables?
Variables made outside every function, visible everywhere. Easy now, painful later: any function can change them. Static locals and globals, next, shows them and the bug they cause.
Why is this a good thing?
You can read one function without worrying that some other function is secretly changing its variables.
rungs.bridge: You know where variables live. Next: Static locals and globals: a variable that remembers between calls, and one every function can see.

rungs.title: Static locals and globals
rungs.builds: Scope: where a variable lives (locals vanish when the function returns). Functions: parameters and return values.
rungs.why: Some values must outlive one call: how many enemies have spawned, which wave you're on. A normal local is wiped every time its function returns. static keeps a local alive between calls, and a global is one value every function shares. Both are useful, and globals are easy to overuse.

parts: When a value has to last

Locals vanish when their function returns, as Scope showed. Usually that's what you want. Sometimes a value has to outlive one call: how many enemies have spawned so far, which wave the game is on. C gives you two tools. A static local lasts for the whole run but only its own function can see it. A global lasts for the whole run and every function can see it.
static: a local that remembers

Put static in front of a local and it changes how long the box lasts, not who can see it:

  • It's created once, before main starts, and kept until the program ends.
  • Its initialiser runs that one time. static int spawned = 0; does not reset spawned on every call.
  • The name still only works inside its function.
  • With no initialiser it starts at 0, not garbage.

In the program below, fresh is an ordinary local and spawned is static. Watch which one climbs.
Globals: outside every function

A variable declared outside every function, usually near the top of the file, is a global. Every function below it can read it and change it. Like a static, it's created before main starts, lasts the whole run and starts at 0 if you don't give it a value. In the program below, main changes wave and spawn_enemy sees the new value without being passed anything.
The shared-counter bug

That “anyone can change it” is the danger. Here two functions both count with a global i:

int i;

void draw_row(void) {
    for (i = 0; i < WIDTH; i++) {
        printf(".");
    }
    printf("\n");
}

void draw_map(void) {
    for (i = 0; i < ROWS; i++) {
        draw_row();
    }
}

With WIDTH 10 and ROWS 3 you get one row, not three. draw_map sets i to 0 and calls draw_row, which runs i up to 10. Back in draw_map, i++ makes it 11, 11 < 3 is false, and the map is done. No warning, no crash, just a wrong picture. The fix is for (int i = 0; ...) in each loop and no global i at all.
Why our starters use them sparingly

When a global holds a wrong value, any function in the file could have put it there, so every function is a suspect. A function that only uses its parameters can be read, tested and reused on its own. The habit in this course: pass values in, return them out, and reach for a global only when that can't work. The Win32 starters in Phase 5 keep a few, because Windows calls your code back in a way that won't let you pass extras.
MSVC notes

A local or parameter with the same name as a global is C4459 under /W4, so /WX stops the build. A global called score means no other function can have a score. Give globals names that won't collide. static in front of a function or a global means something else (private to the file). That's in Organising Code (Phase 3.75).

walk: A global: declared outside every function, so every function below can use it. It's made before main runs and lasts the whole program.
static makes spawned last between calls. The = 0 happens once, before main starts, not on every call.
An ordinary local. A brand-new fresh, set to 0, is made on every call and thrown away at the closing brace.
spawned keeps last call's value, so it climbs: 1, then 2, then 3.
fresh started at 0 again, so this always makes it 1.
spawn_enemy reads the global wave without being passed it.
main changes the global. The next call sees 2.
rungs.model: Mental model: a local is chalk on a meeting-room whiteboard, wiped when the meeting ends. A static local is a tally sheet in that room's locked drawer: still there next meeting, and only that room has the key. A global is the scoreboard in the corridor: everyone can read it, and anyone can change it.

check.q: What is the last line printed?
check.hint: Which of spawned and fresh survives between calls? And what did main do to wave before the third call?
check.why: spawned is static, so it keeps counting across calls: 3 by the third. fresh is an ordinary local, made again at 0 each call, so it's always 1. main set the global wave to 2 before the third call, and spawn_enemy sees that.

miss.1: That's what a normal local would do. static int spawned = 0 runs once, so spawned keeps its value between calls.
miss.2: fresh is an ordinary local. It's made again and set to 0 on every call, so it never gets past 1.
miss.3: wave is a global. main changed it to 2 on line 16, and every function sees the change.

tryit.task: Fill the blank so count_frames remembers how many times it has run and returns the new count: 1, then 2, then 3.
tryit.answer: static   (without it, frames is made again at 0 on every call, so it always returns 1)

qa: Doesn't static int spawned = 0 set it back to 0 on every call?
No. A static's initialiser runs once, before main starts. To reset it, write a separate assignment such as spawned = 0; on its own line.
Can main read spawned?
No. static changes how long the box lasts, not who can see it. The name still only works inside spawn_enemy. If main needs the number, have the function return it.
What does a global hold if I don't give it a value?
0. Globals and statics start at 0. Only ordinary locals start as garbage, which is why MSVC warns C4700 about those.
Is a global ever the right choice?

Sometimes: a value the whole program shares that would otherwise be passed to almost every function, or a place Windows code needs to reach from a callback. Start with parameters and return values; move to a global when they really can't do the job.
rungs.bridge: Values can now last as long as you need. Next: Named constants with #define, giving fixed numbers a name.

rungs.title: Named constants with #define
rungs.builds: Variables and types (Phase 2), where #define first named MAX_LIVES. Loops: while and for (Phase 2.5).
rungs.why: A 5 in the middle of your code could mean five scores, five lives or five pixels. #define gives a fixed number a name, so the code says what it means, and you change it in one place.

parts: A find-and-replace before compiling

You met #define in Variables and types. Here's what's really going on. Before the compiler sees your file, a separate step called the preprocessor runs over it. It handles every line starting with #: it pastes in the files named by #include and swaps each #defined name for its text. What comes out is plain C with no # lines left, and that's what the compiler reads.

You can see that output. cl /P define.c writes it to define.i instead of building anything. The file is long, because all of stdio.h is pasted in at the top; scroll to the bottom and your main is there, with 5 where MAX_SCORES was.
Whole names only, and no scope

The swap only touches whole names. With #define MAX 5, the word MAX_SCORES is left alone, and so is MAX inside a string in quotes. A macro also ignores braces. A #define written inside a function works from that line to the end of the file, in every function below it. That's why they all go at the top, where you can see them.
Errors land where the name is used

The preprocessor pastes text without checking it. A mistake in a #define line usually shows up somewhere else:

#define START_LIVES 3;
...
printf("%d\n", START_LIVES);

The printf becomes printf("%d\n", 3;);, and the syntax error is reported on the printf line, not the #define. When an error makes no sense on a line that uses a macro, go and read the macro. The missing-brackets trap from Variables and types is the same problem: the text is pasted in, then the maths happens.
What to name

A macro can hold text as well as numbers: #define SAVE_FILE "scores.txt" keeps the save file's name in one place, ready for Files at the end of this phase. A good rule is to name every number except 0 and 1. A 0 that starts a count or a 1 that adds one explains itself. A 5, a 32 or a 60 doesn't.
Another way: enum

You'll also see enum { MAX_SCORES = 5 };. That makes a real int constant the compiler knows about, so it follows scope, shows its name in the debugger and can still size an array. It only works for whole numbers. Organising Code (Phase 3.75) covers enum properly; for now, #define is fine.

walk: #define MAX_SCORES 5: before compiling, every MAX_SCORES in the file is swapped for 5. No = and no ;.
Names go in capitals by convention, so you can tell a constant from a variable at a glance.
Reads as “start with the starting lives”, not “start with 3”.
The loop runs MAX_SCORES times. Change line 3 to 10 and every use updates.
rungs.model: Mental model: find-and-replace that runs before the compiler. The compiler never sees MAX_SCORES, only the 5 it was swapped for.

check.q: How many “Slot” lines print, and what is the last one?
check.hint: Count the values i takes before i < MAX_SCORES stops the loop.
check.why: i goes 0, 1, 2, 3, 4: five lines, and the last is Slot 4. When i reaches 5, i < 5 fails. Counting from 0 is how arrays work too, which is next.

miss.0: i stops before reaching 5, because the loop needs i < 5.
miss.3: The loop stops when i reaches 5, so 5 never prints.

tryit.task: Replace the magic number with a named constant.

qa: Why does #define have no = or ;?
It isn’t C code. It’s an instruction to the preprocessor, which runs before the compiler. A ; would get pasted in everywhere the name is used and cause odd errors.
#define or const int?
const int MAX = 5; has a type and works for most things, but in C (unlike C++) it can’t size an array: int scores[MAX]; fails in MSVC. That’s why array sizes use #define. Both beat a bare 5.
What else does the preprocessor do?
#include is one too: it pastes a whole file in. You can see the result with cl /P. Organising Code (Phase 3.75) adds #pragma once.
What goes wrong with #define WIDTH 80 + 2?
It’s find-and-replace, so WIDTH * 2 becomes 80 + 2 * 2, which is 84, not 164. Put brackets around anything with an operator: #define WIDTH (80 + 2).
Why are #define names in capitals?
It’s a convention, not a rule. Capitals tell you at a glance that it’s a fixed value, not a variable that changes while the game runs.
rungs.bridge: Your numbers have names. Next: arrays, many values under one name.

rungs.title: Arrays: many values, one name
rungs.kick: int a[5] · a[0] · loop to count - 1
rungs.builds: Named constants with #define for the size. Loops: while and for (Phase 2.5). Division, remainder and casts (Phase 2) for the (int) cast.
rungs.why: Five high scores in five variables is clumsy, and fifty is impossible. An array is a row of boxes under one name, numbered from 0. Pair it with a for loop and the same few lines handle any number of values.

parts: A row of boxes under one name

An array is a fixed number of boxes of one type, side by side in memory, sharing one name. int scores[5]; makes five ints. You reach each box by its index, its position counted from 0, so the five boxes are scores[0] to scores[4]. The size in the brackets must be a constant, which is why it's usually a #define.
Each element is an ordinary variable

scores[2] behaves exactly like an int variable. You can assign it, add to it with +=, use ++ on it, and read into it with scanf("%d", &scores[i]), the same & as any other int. The index can be any int expression: a loop counter, count - 1, even a character. A char is a small number, so letters can pick a box:

int presses[26] = {0};
presses[key - 'a']++;   /* 'a' is box 0, 'z' is box 25 */
Filling it at the start

An initialiser in braces fills the boxes in order. If it's shorter than the array, the rest are set to 0, so int scores[5] = {0}; is the usual way to start with every box at 0. More values than boxes won't build. Leave the size out and C counts for you: int lanes[] = {1, 2, 3}; has three boxes. With no initialiser at all, a local array is full of garbage, just like a plain local.

For a table that should never change, add const: const int lane_y[3] = {40, 80, 120};. Any line that tries to change it stops the build.
Going past the end

C never checks an index. scores[5] in a five-box array reads or writes whatever sits next in memory, maybe another variable like lives. Nothing stops it and nothing reports it: lives just changes, and the bug shows up somewhere else. The classic cause is i <= count where it should be i < count.
Copying an array

backup = scores; doesn't build: an array name isn't a box you can assign to (C2106). Copy element by element with a loop, or use memcpy(backup, scores, sizeof(scores)); from <string.h>, which copies the bytes in one call. Both arrays must be the same type and size.
MSVC notes

sizeof gives a size_t, so the count line in the program below casts it with (int) to keep /W4 quiet. MSVC won't warn about scores[i] going out of range, and only sometimes about a fixed scores[5]. It also has no variable-length arrays: int scores[n]; won't build.

walk: int scores[MAX_SCORES] makes five int boxes in a row. The braces fill them in order.
sizeof(scores) is the whole array in bytes (20). sizeof(scores[0]) is one element (4). 20 / 4 = 5. The (int) cast from Phase 2 keeps /W4 quiet.
The first box is [0], not [1].
The last box is [4]: count - 1. It changes from 10 to 25 here.
The standard array loop: start at 0, stop before count.
scores[i] is whichever box i points at this time round.
rungs.model: Mental model: a row of lockers numbered from 0. scores[2] means locker 2, which is the third one. Five lockers are numbered 0 to 4. There is no locker 5.

check.q: What is the last line printed?
check.hint: Line 10 changed one box before the loop runs. Which one, and what does the loop print for it?
check.why: The loop prints i + 1 as the position, so the last line is position 5, which is scores[4]. Line 10 changed it from 10 to 25 before the loop ran.

miss.0: scores[4] was changed to 25 on line 10, before the loop.
miss.2: The loop prints i + 1, so the last position is 5.
miss.3: 40 is scores[3]. The last element is scores[4].

tryit.task: Finish the loop that finds the highest score.

qa: What happens if I use scores[5]?
C doesn’t check. It reads or writes whatever memory sits after the array: garbage at best, a crash or a corrupted variable at worst, and no error message. Keep loops at i < count.
Why start counting at 0?
The number is how far a box is from the start. The first box is 0 steps along. It feels odd for a week, then it’s natural.
Can the size be a variable?
Use a #define or a fixed number for array sizes in this roadmap. C99 added variable-size arrays, MSVC never supported them, and C11 made them optional, so stick to fixed sizes.
Where do games use arrays?
Anywhere there are many of something: Enemy enemies[10], Bullet bullets[64], int scores[5], bool keys[256], char name[32]. Each is walked with the same for loop.
Does passing an array to a function copy it?
No, and that surprises everyone once. The function works on your real array. Passing arrays to functions, next, shows how, and why the length has to be passed separately.
rungs.bridge: You can store a row of numbers. Next: Passing arrays to functions, handing a whole table to a function.

rungs.title: Passing arrays to functions
rungs.kick: int a[] + count · no copy · const · capacity
rungs.builds: Arrays: many values, one name. Functions: parameters and return values. Scope (an int argument is a copy).
rungs.why: The high-score table needs functions that print it, add a score and shift the rest down, and they all need the array. C passes arrays in a way that surprises everyone once: the function works on your real array, and it can't tell how long it is. Know both and the table is easy.

parts: Hand over the array and its count

To give a function a whole array, write the parameter with empty brackets and pass the count as a second parameter:

void add_bonus(int scores[], int count, int bonus)

At the call, use the array's name on its own, with no brackets and no &: add_bonus(scores, count, 5);. The count has to travel with the array, because inside the function there's no way to find the length out.
The function works on your array

An int argument is copied, as Scope showed. An array isn't. Passing the name hands over where the array lives, so the function opens the same boxes as main. Write scores[0] += 5; inside add_bonus and main's scores[0] changes. That's useful: one function can fill, sort or update a table for you, and nothing gets copied, however big the array is. Why C works this way is finished in Pointers and arrays, in Phase 3.5.
sizeof doesn't work in here

The count trick from Arrays only works in the function where the array was declared:

void show_count(int scores[]) {
    printf("%zu\n", sizeof(scores) / sizeof(scores[0]));
}

Pass it a five-box array and it prints 2. Inside the function, scores holds only the array's location, which takes 8 bytes on x64, and 8 / 4 is 2.

MSVC builds this without a word, even at /W4. That's why the count is always a parameter.
A number in the brackets is ignored

You can write int scores[5] as a parameter, but the compiler throws the 5 away. A three-box array passes without complaint, and the function can't tell. Write [], so the code doesn't promise a check that never happens.
const: a promise not to change it

A function that only reads the array should say so: void print_scores(const int scores[], int count). Now a line inside it that writes to scores stops the build. Anyone reading the first line knows print_scores looks and add_bonus changes.
Count versus capacity

Two numbers describe a table. Capacity is how many boxes exist: MAX_SCORES, fixed when you compile. Count is how many hold real data right now. The high-score table in this phase uses both. insert_score(int scores[], int count, int new_score) loops up to count, and count never goes past MAX_SCORES. Before adding to a table that isn't full yet, check count < MAX_SCORES.

walk: The parameter int scores[] takes an array of any length. count comes separately, because the function has no other way to know how many boxes to use.
This writes straight into main's array. There's no copy: these are main's boxes.
const promises print_scores only reads. Try scores[i] = 0; in here and the build stops.
Capacity 5, three filled. The two left over are set to 0.
count says how many boxes hold real scores. The loops use count, not MAX_SCORES.
Just the name, no brackets and no &. add_bonus gets where main's array lives.
print_scores shows main's array, and it has changed: 45, 100, 65.
rungs.model: Mental model: lending someone the key to your row of lockers, not photocopying what's inside. Whatever they put in a locker is there when you look. The count is a note saying how many lockers are in use, because the key doesn't tell them.

opts: Nothing: it won't build, because count is 3 and the array holds 5
check.hint: Does add_bonus get a copy of the scores, or main's actual boxes? And where do both loops stop?
check.why: add_bonus writes into main's array, so each of the three scores goes up by 5. print_scores then reads main's array. Both loops stop at count, 3, so the two spare boxes are never touched or printed.

miss.1: That's how a single int argument behaves. An array isn't copied, so add_bonus changed main's scores.
miss.2: Both loops stop at count, which is 3. The two spare boxes are never touched or printed.
miss.3: Count and capacity are allowed to differ. MAX_SCORES is how many boxes exist; count is how many are in use.

tryit.task: Fill the blanks: clear_scores sets the first count scores to 0, and main calls it on its scores array.
tryit.answer: int   then   scores   (just the name: no brackets, no &)

qa: Why can't the function work out the length with sizeof?
Inside the function the parameter holds only where the array lives. On x64 that's 8 bytes, so sizeof(scores) / sizeof(scores[0]) gives 2 whatever you passed, and MSVC doesn't warn. Pass the count.
Do I need an & like with scanf?
No. The array's name already hands over where it lives. add_bonus(&scores, ...) is wrong.
What if I pass just scores[2]?
That's one int, and it's copied like any int. The function can read it, but changing it won't touch main's array.
Can a function return an array?
No, as Functions said. The C habit is the other way round: the caller makes the array and passes it in, and the function fills it.
Why does it work this way?
Copying a big array on every call would be slow, so C passes its location instead. The full story, and what that location really is, comes in Pointers and arrays (Phase 3.5).
rungs.bridge: Your functions can share arrays. Next: strings, which are arrays of characters with one twist.

rungs.title: Strings and the '\0' at the end
rungs.builds: Arrays: many values, one name, and Passing arrays to functions. From Phase 2: char, and %zu from How big a number can be.
rungs.why: C has no string type. A string is a char array, and C marks where the text ends with a hidden character, '\0'. Every string function relies on finding it. Knowing it’s there explains most string bugs before they happen.

parts: A char array with a stop sign

C has no string type. Text lives in a char array, and the character '\0', whose value is 0, marks where the text ends. printf's %s, strlen and every function in string.h walk along the array until they reach that byte. So an array's size and its string's length are two different numbers: sizeof counts the boxes you reserved, strlen counts the letters before the stop sign.
Size it as letters + 1

A string always needs one box more than its longest text. Name the letter count, and add the 1 where you make the array, so the reason stays on screen:

#define NAME_MAX 15          /* longest name, in letters */
char name[NAME_MAX + 1];     /* + 1 for the '\0' */

Some code names the whole buffer instead, like the starter's NAME_LEN 32, which already counts the '\0'. Either style works if the name says which one it is. Mixing them up is how you end up one box short.
How quoted text fills an array

Text in double quotes is a string literal, and it always brings a hidden '\0' with it, so "Sam" takes 4 bytes. Three ways to start an array from one:

  • char a[8] = "Sam"; stores S, a, m, '\0', and C zeros the other four boxes.
  • char b[] = "Sam"; lets C count: 4 boxes. sizeof(b) is 4, strlen(b) is 3.
  • char c[3] = "Sam"; has room for the letters and nothing else, so C quietly drops the '\0'.

That last one is legal C, but c is not a string. MSVC spots it at /W4 (C4295, array too small for the terminating null), and /WX stops the build; many other compilers say nothing. Print it with %s and you get Sam plus whatever bytes follow. When the number in the brackets equals the letter count, the terminator is gone.
Lining up columns

A number between the % and the s sets a width. %10s pads on the left, so the text ends at column 10. %-10s pads on the right, which is what a name column wants:

printf("%-10s%6d\n", "Sam", 1200);
printf("%-10s%6d\n", "Alexandra", 950);

Names line up on the left edge and scores on the right. A name longer than the width isn't cut off; it just pushes that row out of line.
Quoted text is read-only

Your own array is yours to change: the program below swaps one letter with name[1] = 'u'. The literal in quotes is different. The compiler may keep it in memory your program can only read, and writing to it is undefined behaviour. char name[8] = "Sam"; is safe because it copies the letters into your array first. Phase 3.5 shows the risky way to point at a literal, and why to avoid it.
Not every char array is a string

The '\0' only matters to code that looks for it. A char map[3][5] level, printed one tile at a time with %c by a loop that counts columns, never needs one. 2D arrays: grids draws exactly that kind of map. Add a terminator when %s, strlen or another string function will read the array.

strlen and sizeof both give a size_t. Print them with %zu, as in How big a number can be, or cast to int for %d. A bare %d with a size_t is a format mismatch under /W4 (C4477), and /WX stops the build.
learn.king: §13.1–13.4 (skip “Character Arrays versus Character Pointers” in §13.2 until Phase 3.5)

walk: string.h has the string tools: strlen, strcmp and more.
Eight char boxes. "Sam" fills the first three, and C puts '\0' in box 3 to mark the end. The rest are zero too.
%s prints characters until it reaches the '\0'.
strlen counts characters up to the '\0', not counting it: 3.
sizeof is the whole array: 8 boxes, however much text is in it.
A string is an array, so you can change one character. Box 1 becomes u.
rungs.model: Mental model: a row of boxes with a stop sign after the last letter. Everything that reads a string walks along until it hits the stop sign. Lose the sign and it keeps walking into memory that isn’t yours.

check.q: What does the last printf show?
check.hint: Which box is name[1]? Arrays count from 0.
check.why: name[0] is S, name[1] is a, name[2] is m. Line 9 replaces the a with u, giving Sum.

miss.0: Line 9 changed one character before the last printf.
miss.1: Assigning replaces a box. It doesn’t insert one.
miss.2: name[1] is the second box, not the first.

tryit.task: How many letters can char name[32] hold? Fill in, then check by printing strlen of a long name.
tryit.code: // char name[32] holds at most ____ letters, because ____
tryit.answer: 31, because one box is needed for the '\0' at the end.

qa: Why can’t I write name = "Alex"; later?
Arrays can’t be assigned with = after they’re made. Copying and joining strings, two concepts on, shows the safe way to put text into an array. Reading it from the keyboard with fgets comes next.
What’s the difference between 'a' and "a"?
'a' is one char. "a" is a string: two boxes, 'a' and '\0'.
What if a string has no '\0'?
%s and strlen keep reading past the end until they happen to find a zero byte. You get garbage or a crash. The weekly “string with no end” exercise shows it.
Is '\0' the same as the character '0'?
No. '\0' has the value 0. '0' is the printable digit, with the value 48. printf("%d %d\n", '\0', '0'); prints 0 48.
rungs.bridge: You know what a string really is. Next: Reading a line of text with fgets, so the player can type a name.

rungs.title: Reading a line of text with fgets
rungs.builds: Strings and the '\0' at the end. Reading input with scanf (Phase 2), and the getchar loop from do, break, continue and the endless loop (Phase 2.5).
rungs.why: scanf("%s") stops at the first space and doesn’t know how big your array is, so a long name overflows it. fgets reads a whole line and never writes more than the size you give it. It’s the safe way to read a name.

parts: Three streams

Every C program starts with three streams already open, declared in stdio.h:

  • stdin, standard input: the keyboard, unless input comes from a file.
  • stdout, standard output: where printf writes.
  • stderr, standard error: a second route to the screen, kept for error messages.

fgets takes the stream as its last argument, so the same call reads a line typed at the keyboard or, in Saving and loading with files, a line from a file.
What fgets does

fgets(buf, size, stdin) copies characters into buf until one of three things happens: it has stored size - 1 of them, it has stored the \n from Enter, or the input runs out. Then it adds the '\0'. It never writes past the last box, which is why it's safe where scanf("%s") isn't.

It returns NULL when it couldn't read anything: the input has ended (Ctrl+Z then Enter in a Windows console) or something went wrong. The array can't be trusted then, so check the result before using it. The program below does that on line 7.
A line that was too long

If the player types more than size - 1 characters, fgets stops early and the rest of the line waits in stdin. You can spot it, because the buffer has no \n in it. Throw the leftovers away with the getchar loop from do, break, continue and the endless loop:

size_t end = strcspn(name, "\n");
if (name[end] == '\n') {
    name[end] = '\0';         /* normal line: drop the Enter */
} else {
    int c;                    /* too long: eat the rest */
    while ((c = getchar()) != '\n' && c != EOF) { }
}

Skip this and the next fgets quietly reads the tail of the old line.
Numbers: fgets, then sscanf

Mixing scanf("%d") and fgets goes wrong because scanf leaves the Enter behind, and the next fgets sees it as an empty line. The tidy habit is to read every answer as a line, then pull the number out with sscanf, which works like scanf but reads from a string:

char line[16];
int lane = 0;
if (fgets(line, sizeof(line), stdin) != NULL &&
    sscanf(line, "%d", &lane) == 1) {
    printf("Lane %d\n", lane);
}

The whole line is used up either way, so typing abc can't jam the next read.
Two things to leave alone

fflush(stdin) turns up in old tutorials as a way to clear typed input. The C standard only defines fflush for output; on an input stream the result is undefined, and Microsoft's library has changed how it treats it over the years. Use the getchar loop instead.

gets, the old line reader with no size argument, overflowed so easily that C11 removed it from the language, and Visual Studio 2015 dropped it too. Any example that uses it is out of date.
MSVC notes
fgets builds clean under /W4. sscanf doesn't: MSVC flags it with C4996, just like scanf, so a file that uses it needs #define _CRT_SECURE_NO_WARNINGS as its very first line for now.

walk: Room for 31 letters plus the '\0'.

fgets(where, how much, from where): read a line into name, never more than sizeof(name) - 1 characters plus the '\0', from stdin, the keyboard. It returns NULL if nothing could be read, for example when input has ended.
No line means nothing to work with, so main gives up and returns 1.
The brackets show exactly what’s in name. fgets keeps the Enter, so the ] lands on the next line.
strcspn finds the position of the first \n. Putting '\0' there ends the string before it. Every fgets gets this line straight after.
Now the brackets close right after the name.
rungs.model: Mental model: fgets is a scoop with a size limit. It scoops the whole line, Enter included, and never overflows the cup. The strcspn line wipes the Enter off the bottom.

check.q: The player types Sam and presses Enter. What does line 10 print?
check.hint: What is in name before line 11 runs?
check.why: fgets stores S, a, m and the \n from Enter, so the ] prints on the next line. Line 11 removes that \n, which is why line 12 prints [Sam].

miss.1: That’s line 12, after the newline is stripped.
miss.2: Enter is stored as \n, a new line, not a space.
miss.3: The Enter comes after the letters you typed, not before them.

tryit.task: Read a player tag of up to 15 letters safely and strip the newline.

qa: Why not scanf("%s", name)?
It stops at the first space, so “Sam Taylor” becomes “Sam”, and it has no idea how big name is. Type 50 letters into 32 boxes and it writes past the end. MSVC flags it with C4996 for that reason.
What if they type more than 31 letters?

fgets stops at 31 and leaves the rest waiting in the input. Your array is safe, but the next read picks up the leftovers. The Learn it part “A line that was too long” shows how to spot that and throw them away.
Mixing scanf("%d") and fgets?
scanf leaves the Enter behind, and the next fgets reads it as an empty line. Read every answer with fgets and pull numbers out with sscanf, as in “Numbers: fgets, then sscanf” above.
rungs.bridge: You can read a name safely. Next: Copying and joining strings, because = won’t put text into an array.

rungs.title: Copying and joining strings
rungs.builds: Strings and the '\0' at the end, Reading a line of text with fgets, and printf's format codes from Printing values with printf (Phase 2).
rungs.why: You'll want to put a player's name into the high-score table, or build a line like “Alexandr scored 4500” for the screen. = can't copy text into an array, and the classic copy functions trust you to have made the array big enough. snprintf copies and joins text, never writes past the size you give it, and tells you when something didn't fit.

parts: Why = won't copy text

An array's name isn't something you can assign to. name = "Alex"; and name = other; both fail to compile; MSVC reports C2106 (the left side must be an l-value). Copying text means copying characters one box at a time, then the '\0'. string.h has functions that do it, and each one has a catch.
strcpy and strcat: no size check

strcpy(dest, src) copies src and its terminator into dest. strcat(dest, src) finds the '\0' in dest and copies src on from there. Neither knows how big dest is. Copy a 20-letter name into char name[9] and strcpy writes 12 bytes past the end, over whatever sits next to it. No error, no warning: just a wrong score or a crash later on.
The n versions have their own traps

strncpy(dest, src, n) copies at most n characters. If src has n or more, it stops without writing a '\0', and dest isn't a string. You have to add one yourself, every time:

strncpy(name, typed, NAME_MAX);
name[NAME_MAX] = '\0';

strncat(dest, src, n) adds at most n characters and then always writes a '\0'. So n must be the space left minus one: sizeof(dest) - strlen(dest) - 1. Passing sizeof(dest) is the usual mistake, and it can overflow.
snprintf: the one to reach for

snprintf(dest, size, format, ...) is printf into an array. It never writes more than size bytes, and it always finishes with a '\0' (unless size is 0). One tool covers both jobs:

snprintf(name, sizeof(name), "%s", typed);           /* copy */
snprintf(line, sizeof(line), "%s: %d", name, score); /* join */

Copy with "%s" as the format rather than passing the text itself: a % in a player's name would be read as an instruction. The return value is the length the full text would have had. If it's size or more, the text was cut short. The program below checks exactly that.
MSVC notes

MSVC flags strcpy, strcat, strncpy and strncat with C4996 and points you at its own strcpy_s family. A file that uses them needs #define _CRT_SECURE_NO_WARNINGS as its first line, as in Saving and loading with files. snprintf isn't flagged, so the program below doesn't need that line. Steer clear of _snprintf with an underscore: it's an older Microsoft function that leaves out the '\0' when the text doesn't fit and returns -1, which is the very bug snprintf fixes.

walk: NAME_MAX is the longest name, in letters. The array on line 7 adds 1 for the '\0'.
Pretend this came from fgets: 9 letters, more than the table allows.
NAME_MAX + 1 is 9 boxes: 8 letters and the stop sign.

snprintf(where, size, format, ...) is printf into name, never writing more than sizeof(name) bytes. "%s" copies typed as plain text. 8 letters and the '\0' fit. It returns 9, the length the whole name would have had.
If the wanted length is the size or more, something was cut. 9 >= 9, so yes. The (int) cast matches sizeof's size_t to need's int.
Joining: name, some words and a number go into line in one call. 20 letters fit easily in 32 boxes.
line is an ordinary string now, so %s prints it.
rungs.model: Mental model: snprintf is printf with a box count. It writes what fits, always keeps one box for the stop sign, and tells you how much it wanted to write, so you can see when it ran out of room.

check.hint: name has 9 boxes. How many of them does the '\0' need?
check.why: snprintf keeps one box for the '\0', so 8 letters fit: Alexandr. The final a is dropped, and the return value of 9 is how line 12 knows.

miss.0: Alexandra needs 10 boxes with its '\0', and name only has 9.
miss.2: Only one box is held back, for the '\0'. That leaves room for 8 letters.
miss.3: snprintf always writes the '\0', even when it has to cut the text short. That's what makes it safer than strncpy.

tryit.task: Build a label like “Sam (lv 3)” from a tag and a level, and print a warning if it didn't fit.

qa: Can I use strcpy if I know the text fits?

Yes. Copying one row of a names table into another row the same size can never overflow, and 2D arrays: grids does exactly that. The danger is text from outside, like a typed name or a line from a file: you don't decide how long it is. Use snprintf for those. Remember strcpy needs the _CRT_SECURE_NO_WARNINGS line under MSVC.
Why the "%s" instead of passing the name straight in?
The third argument is a format. If the name held a %, snprintf would treat it as an instruction and go looking for a value that isn't there. "%s" says “copy this text exactly as it is”.
Can snprintf fail completely?
It returns a negative number on an encoding error. That's rare with plain text, and need >= (int)sizeof(name) doesn't catch it. Careful code writes if (need < 0 || need >= (int)sizeof(name)).
What about strcpy_s and strcat_s?

They're what MSVC's C4996 message suggests, and they do take a size. They come from an optional part of the C standard that almost only Microsoft ships, so code using them won't build on most other compilers. snprintf works everywhere.
rungs.bridge: You can copy and join text safely. Next: Comparing strings with strcmp, because == doesn't compare letters either.

rungs.title: Comparing strings with strcmp
rungs.builds: Strings and the '\0' at the end, Reading a line of text with fgets, and Copying and joining strings.
rungs.why: You’ll want to check if the player typed “quit”, or if a name is already on the high-score table. == on two strings compares where they live in memory, not their letters. strcmp compares the letters.

parts: Dictionary order, by character code

strcmp walks both strings side by side and stops at the first place they differ, or at the end. The answer comes from those two characters' codes. Capitals sit before small letters in the character table ('Z' is 90, 'a' is 97), so "Zed" sorts before "apple". If one string runs out first, it sorts first: "Sam" before "Samuel".
Only the sign means anything

The result is negative, zero or positive. The standard doesn't say which negative number, so test < 0, == 0 or > 0, never == -1. MSVC tends to give -1 and 1; other libraries give the gap between the two characters.
Just the start: strncmp
strncmp(a, b, n) compares at most n characters. strncmp(cmd, "go", 2) == 0 is true for go, gold and goblin, which suits a command where the player can type more after it.
Ignoring case with toupper

toupper, from <ctype.h>, turns one letter into a capital and leaves anything else alone. Uppercase the text, then compare:

for (int i = 0; cmd[i] != '\0'; i++) {
    cmd[i] = (char)toupper((unsigned char)cmd[i]);
}

The (unsigned char) cast matters. MSVC's char is signed, so a letter like é can be negative, and giving toupper a negative value is undefined. The (char) on the outside keeps /W4 quiet about storing an int in a char.
MSVC notes

if (name == "Sam") is C4130 under /W4 (logical operation on address of string constant), so /WX stops the build. That's MSVC telling you to use strcmp. toupper returns an int, so storing it straight into a char is C4244; the (char) cast above is what keeps the build clean.

walk: strcmp returns 0 when the two strings match exactly. So “equal” is == 0, which reads backwards at first.
It returns a negative number when the first string sorts earlier. apple is before banana, so this is true: 1.
Capitals are different characters. Sam and sam don’t match: 0.
rungs.model: Mental model: strcmp answers “how do these two words sort?”, not “are they the same?”. Negative: the first comes first. Zero: same. Positive: the first comes later. Same is just the zero case.

check.q: What does if (strcmp(cmd, "quit")) { … } do when cmd is "quit"?
check.hint: What number does strcmp return for a match, and how does if treat that number?
check.why: A match returns 0, and if treats 0 as false, so the block is skipped. It runs for every string except "quit". Always write == 0 for “equal”.

miss.0: strcmp gives 0 for a match, and if (0) is false.
miss.1: It compiles. It’s a logic bug, not a syntax error.
miss.3: An if runs its block at most once.

tryit.task: Print “Welcome back” only when the name is Sam.

qa: Why doesn’t == work on strings?

name == "Sam" compares two memory addresses, not letters, so it would never be true. Under your /W4 build MSVC catches it as C4130 (logical operation on address of string constant), and /WX stops the build. Phase 3.5 explains addresses.
How do I ignore capitals?
Uppercase the text with toupper, as in the Learn it above, then compare. MSVC also has _stricmp(a, b), which ignores case in one call, but it’s Windows-only.
Does strcmp care about the \n from fgets?
Yes. "Sam\n" isn’t "Sam". That’s why you strip the newline straight after fgets.
rungs.bridge: You can work with text. Next: 2D arrays: grids, rows and columns like a game map.

rungs.title: 2D arrays: grids
rungs.builds: Arrays: many values, one name, and Passing arrays to functions. Loops inside loops from Loops: while and for (Phase 2.5). The name-shifting example uses Copying and joining strings.
rungs.why: A level map, a tile grid or a board is rows and columns. A 2D array is an array of rows. Two loops, one inside the other, visit every cell.

parts: Rows of rows

A 2D array is an array whose elements are arrays. char map[3][5] is 3 rows of 5 chars, stored one row after another: all of row 0, then all of row 1. map[r][c] picks row r, then column c inside it. Both count from 0, so the last cell is map[2][4].
Filling it

Nested braces fill it row by row, as in the program below. int hits[3][5] = {0}; sets all 15 cells to 0, because anything you leave out is zeroed, just as with a one-row array. A local 2D array with no initialiser holds garbage, like any other local.
m[i, j] is a trap

Some languages write a cell as m[i, j]. In C that means something else: the comma is an operator that works out i, throws it away and keeps j. So map[1, 3] is really map[3], a whole row, and with only 3 rows it's off the end too. You might get a type warning, or nothing that points at the real mistake. Always write two pairs of brackets.
Passing a grid to a function

A function can take a 2D array, but the column count has to be in the parameter: void draw(char map[][COLS], int rows). To reach map[r][c] the compiler skips r whole rows, so it must know how long a row is. The row count can be left empty and passed on its own, just like the count in Passing arrays to functions.
Rows of text: shifting names down

char names[5][16] is five strings, one per row. Version 2 of the high-score table (the stretch goal, with names) makes room for a new name by moving each row below the slot down by one, starting from the bottom so nothing is overwritten before it moves:

for (int i = MAX_SCORES - 1; i > slot; i--) {
    strcpy(names[i], names[i - 1]);
    scores[i] = scores[i - 1];
}
snprintf(names[slot], sizeof(names[slot]), "%s", name);

strcpy is safe here: every row is the same size, so one row always fits in the next. The new name came from the player, so it goes in with snprintf. strcpy needs the C4996 line at the top, as Copying and joining strings explains.
Check both indexes

C checks neither index. map[1][7] doesn't fail: rows sit end to end, so it lands in row 2 (and officially it's undefined behaviour). Before a player's move touches a cell, test both: if (r >= 0 && r < ROWS && c >= 0 && c < COLS). A wall round the edge of the map, like the # border below, is a bounds check the player can see.
learn.king: §8.2 (2D parameters are in §9.3; arrays of strings open §13.7)

walk: map[ROWS][COLS]: 3 rows of 5 chars. The first number is the row.
Row 1 is the middle row. P sits at column 2.
map[1][3]: row 1, column 3. The dot to the right of P becomes E.
The outer loop picks a row.
The inner loop walks across that row’s columns.
After each row, a new line.
rungs.model: Mental model: a spreadsheet. map[row][column], always row first. The outer loop moves down, the inner loop moves across.

check.hint: map[1][3] is row 1, column 3. Count columns from 0 along the middle row.
check.why: The middle row is # . P . # at columns 0 to 4. Column 3 is the second dot, so it becomes E: #.PE#.

miss.1: Column 3 is to the right of P, not the left.

qa: Why row first?
It’s how C lays out the memory: all of row 0, then all of row 1. Looping rows on the outside walks memory in order.
Can I pass a 2D array to a function?

Yes, with the column count in the parameter: void draw(char map[][COLS], int rows). “Passing a grid to a function” above explains why. The runner in Phase 4.5 uses a single row instead, which is simpler.
How is this different from an array of strings?
Very close. char names[5][32] is five strings of up to 31 letters. Each row is one string.

rungs.title: Saving and loading with files
rungs.builds: Printing values with printf and Reading input with scanf (Phase 2): the file versions work the same way. The stdin, stdout and stderr streams from Reading a line of text with fgets.
rungs.why: When your program ends, every variable is gone. Writing to a file keeps a value between runs, like a best score. The stretch goal uses exactly this.

parts: A file is a stream too

fopen connects your program to a file on disk and hands back a FILE *, a handle you pass to every other file function. Read it as “the file I opened”; Phase 3.5 explains the *. Once it's open, fprintf and fscanf work just like printf and scanf, with the handle as the first argument. When you're finished, fclose writes out anything still waiting and lets go of the file.
Modes and paths

The second argument to fopen says what you want:

  • "r": read. The file must exist, or fopen returns NULL.
  • "w": write. Creates the file, or empties an existing one the moment it opens.
  • "a": append. Creates it if needed, and every write goes on the end.
  • "r+", "w+", "a+": read and write, with the same create and empty rules as their first letter.
  • Add b ("rb", "wb") for binary mode, covered at the end.

A bare name like "best.txt" means the folder you ran the program from, not the folder the .exe sits in. In a full Windows path every backslash is doubled, because \ starts an escape sequence: "C:\\games\\best.txt". Forward slashes work on Windows too: "C:/games/best.txt".
Check every open, close every file

fopen returns NULL when it fails: a missing file in "r" mode, a folder you can't write to, a typo in the name. Passing NULL to fprintf crashes, so test the handle straight after every fopen. Every fopen that works needs exactly one fclose. A program can only hold so many files open at once, and a file that's never closed may never get its last writes.

Error messages go to stderr, as on line 7 below. It shows on screen like stdout but stays separate: if someone runs game.exe > log.txt, normal output goes into the file and the errors still appear in front of them.

A missing file isn't always a mistake. The first time the game runs there's no best.txt yet, so opening it with "r" gives NULL. That's the moment to fall back to a default, and a note on stderr helps while you test:

FILE *f = fopen("best.txt", "r");
if (f == NULL) {
    fprintf(stderr, "No best.txt yet, starting from 0\n");
    best = 0;
}

The program below makes the same check the other way round on line 15: it only reads when the handle isn't NULL.
Buffering: why writes go missing

fprintf doesn't reach the disk straight away. It fills a buffer in memory, and the buffer is written out when it's full, when you call fclose, or when you call fflush(f). If the game crashes first, whatever was still in the buffer is lost, and best.txt can end up empty. For a save file, open, write and close in one go. For a log that must survive a crash, call fflush after the lines that matter.
Reading to the end: the feof trap

The loop everyone writes first is while (!feof(f)), and it's wrong. feof only turns true after a read has already failed, so the loop goes round one extra time and handles the last score twice, or a garbage one. Loop on fscanf's return value instead. It's how many values it filled, so it stops at the end of the file and at a damaged line alike:

int score = 0, total = 0;
while (fscanf(f, "%d", &score) == 1) {
    total += score;
}
Text mode and CR LF

Windows ends each line of a text file with two characters, CR then LF (' ' then ' '). In text mode C translates for you: writing ' ' puts both on disk, and reading turns the pair back into one ' '. Binary mode translates nothing, so a text file read in binary shows a stray ' ' before every ' '. Use text mode for anything you'd open in Notepad.
MSVC notes

MSVC flags fopen and fscanf with C4996 and suggests fopen_s. The program below switches that off with #define _CRT_SECURE_NO_WARNINGS on line 1, before any #include. That line doesn't make anything safer. Checking for NULL and checking what fscanf returns do.

walk: MSVC calls fopen and fscanf unsafe (C4996). This line hides that warning, and must come first. It doesn’t make the code any safer: checking results (lines 6 and 15) does that.
fopen opens best.txt for writing ("w"), creating it if needed. FILE *f is a handle to the open file. The * is a pointer, explained in Phase 3.5. For now, read it as “the file I opened”.
fopen gives back NULL when it fails, for example in a folder you can’t write to. Always check.
Error messages go to stderr with fprintf. They still show on screen, but stay separate from normal output.
fprintf works like printf, but writes into the file instead of the screen.
fclose finishes writing and lets go of the file.
"r" opens it for reading. If the file doesn’t exist, f is NULL and best stays 0.
fscanf works like scanf, but reads from the file.
rungs.model: Mental model: a notebook in a drawer. fopen takes it out ("w" starts a fresh page, "r" just reads), fprintf and fscanf write and read, fclose puts it back. Forget fclose and the last lines may never reach the page.

tryit.task: Add to the file instead of replacing it, so every score is kept.
tryit.answer: "a" (append). "w" wipes the file each time it opens.

qa: What does "w" do to an existing file?
Empties it straight away, before you write anything. Use "a" to add to the end.
Why return 1?
A non-zero return from main tells Windows the program failed: the same idea as %ERRORLEVEL% in build.bat.
What if best.txt has something that isn’t a number in it?

fscanf gives up and best stays 0, silently. fscanf returns how many values it read, so if (fscanf(f, "%d", &best) != 1) catches a damaged file. The & is the same one scanf needs: Phase 3.5 explains it.
What about binary files and fwrite?

fwrite(&best, sizeof(best), 1, f) copies the raw bytes of a variable into a file opened with "wb", and fread copies them back. It’s fast and exact, but you can’t read the file in Notepad, and it may not load on a different compiler or machine. Text written with fprintf is easier to check and fix, so this course saves as text.
